Finally, we express the vertex operators dual to the light insertions $Z$ and $\bar{Z}$ in terms of the rescaled fluctuation fields $\theta$ and $\phi$ . We begin by expanding $v_{Z}$ in (3.37) to linear order in $\theta$ and $\phi$ :1616 16 Higher orders in $\theta$ do not contribute because $\theta/f_{\theta}\sim e^{\mp\rho}$ as $\rho\to\pm\infty$ . On the other hand, because $\phi/f_{\phi}\to 1$ as $\rho\to\pm\infty$ , the vertex operator has a series of corrections involving higher orders of $\phi$ , $e^{\tau+i\phi_{0}}\lim_{z\to 0}\frac{2g}{z}\left(-\frac{\phi^{2}}{2f_{\phi}}-\frac{i\phi^{3}}{3!f_{\phi}^{2}}+\ldots\right)$ , which are not suppressed. There may be a more convenient choice of coordinates than the one in (3.12)-(3.13) that avoids this undesirable behavior. However, practically speaking, at the order in the large charge expansion that we are considering, we may simply ignore the higher order terms in the vertex operators. Contractions between more than one pair of copies of $\phi$ in different vertex operators involve at least two bulk-to-bulk propagators and are suppressed by $1/g$ . Furthermore, while there is a contribution at the order of interest in the large charge expansion involving the self-contraction between the two copies of $\phi$ in the term $\sim\lim_{z\to 0}\frac{\phi^{2}}{zf_{\phi}}$ , it yields a constant that can be absorbed into the definition of the vertex operator.

$$ \displaystyle v_{Z}(t) \displaystyle=\lim_{z\to 0}\frac{2g}{z}\left[\sin{\theta_{\rm cl}}e^{i\phi_{\rm cl}}+\frac{\cos{\theta_{\rm cl}}}{f_{\theta}}e^{i\phi_{\rm cl}}\theta+i\frac{\sin{\theta_{\rm cl}}}{f_{\phi}}e^{i\phi_{\rm cl}}\phi+\ldots\right] \displaystyle=v_{Z}(t)\rvert_{\Phi_{\rm cl}}+e^{\tau(t)+i\phi_{0}}\lim_{z\to 0}\frac{2g}{z}\left(\theta+i\phi\right)+\ldots. $$

To get to the second line, we used that $\cos{\theta_{\rm cl}}/f_{\theta}\to 1$ and $\sin{\theta_{\rm cl}}/f_{\phi}\to 1$ as $\rho\to\pm\infty$ , which follow from (3.14) and (3.21). Likewise, $v_{\bar{Z}}$ in (3.37) expanded to linear order is

$$ \displaystyle v_{\bar{Z}}(t) \displaystyle=v_{\bar{Z}}(t)\rvert_{\Psi_{\rm cl}}+e^{-\tau(t)-i\phi_{0}}\lim_{z\to 0}\frac{2g}{z}\left(\theta-i\phi\right)+\ldots. $$

Thus, the holographic expression for the leading and first subleading terms in the large charge expansion of the defect correlators in (2.20)-(2.21) is:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\braket{Z(t_{1})\bar{Z}(t_{2})Z^{J}(t_{3})\bar{Z}^{J}(t_{4})}}{\braket{Z^{J}(t_{3})\bar{Z}^{J}(t_{4})}} \displaystyle=v_{Z}(t_{1})\rvert_{\Psi_{\rm cl}}v_{\bar{Z}}(t_{2})\rvert_{\Psi_{\rm cl}}+2e^{\tau(t_{1})-\tau(t_{2})}(W_{\theta\theta}(t_{1},t_{2})+iW_{\phi\theta}(t_{1},t_{2})), \displaystyle\frac{\braket{\bar{Z}(t_{1})Z(t_{2})Z^{J}(t_{3})\bar{Z}^{J}(t_{4})}}{\braket{Z^{J}(t_{3})\bar{Z}^{J}(t_{4})}} \displaystyle=v_{\bar{Z}}(t_{1})\rvert_{\Psi_{\rm cl}}v_{Z}(t_{2})\rvert_{\Psi_{\rm cl}}+2e^{\tau(t_{2})-\tau(t_{1})}(W_{\theta\theta}(t_{1},t_{2})-iW_{\phi\theta}(t_{1},t_{2})), $$

where the boundary-to-boundary propagator $W$ ( $\equiv W_{\theta\theta},W_{\phi\theta}$ ) is again given in terms of the bulk-to-bulk propagator $G$ ( $\equiv G_{\theta\theta},G_{\phi\theta}$ ) by (3.41) with $\Delta=1$ .

Finally, we note from (3.38) that the classical pieces in (3.45)-(3.46) are explicitly:

$$ \displaystyle v_{Z}(t_{1})\rvert_{\Psi_{\rm cl}}v_{\bar{Z}}(t_{2})\rvert_{\Psi_{\rm cl}} \displaystyle=\frac{4g^{2}c^{2}}{t_{12}^{2}}\frac{\chi^{2}}{(1-\chi)^{2}}, \displaystyle v_{\bar{Z}}(t_{1})\rvert_{\Psi_{\rm cl}}v_{Z}(t_{2})\rvert_{\Psi_{\rm cl}} \displaystyle=\frac{4g^{2}c^{2}}{t_{12}^{2}}\chi^{2}. $$

## 4 Computing the Green’s functions

The last step in determining the defect four-point correlators is to compute the boundary-to-boundary propagators. We begin by presenting a general way to express the bulk propagators as integrals over Fourier modes conjugate to the global boundary coordinate, send the bulk points to the boundary, and rewrite the resulting integral representation of the boundary propagator as a series. We then apply the procedure to first compute $W_{yy}$ , which lets us determine $W_{\theta\theta}$ and $W_{\theta\phi}$ via the superconformal Ward identities, and then compute $W_{xx}$ .

### 4.1 Integral and series representations of the propagators

Taking advantage of the symmetry of the classical string in (3.14) under translations in the global time coordinate $\tau$ , we write the $yy$ and $xx$ bulk-to-bulk propagators in their Fourier representations:

$$ \displaystyle G(\rho,\tau;\rho^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})\equiv\frac{1}{4\pi g}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dke^{ik(\tau-\tau^{\prime})}g(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k). $$

Here, $G\equiv G_{yy}$ and $g(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k)\equiv g_{yy}(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k)$ or $G\equiv G_{xx}$ and $g(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k)\equiv g_{xx}(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k)$ .

Noting the explicit form of the d’Alembertian on the classical string worldsheet in global coordinates,

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\mu}\left(\sqrt{\gamma}\gamma^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\nu}\right)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\left(\sqrt{\cosh^{2}{\rho}-c^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\right)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\cosh^{2}{\rho}-c^{2}}}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\tau^{2}}, $$

and substituting the Fourier representations of $G_{yy}$ and $G_{xx}$ into (3.30) and (3.29), we find that $g_{yy}$ and $g_{xx}$ satisfy

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{d}{d\rho}\left(\sqrt{\cosh^{2}{\rho}-c^{2}}\frac{d}{d\rho}\right)-\frac{k^{2}}{\sqrt{\cosh^{2}{\rho}-c^{2}}}-\sqrt{\gamma}m^{2}(\rho)\right)g(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k)=-\delta(\rho-\rho^{\prime}), $$

where $m^{2}\equiv m_{y}^{2}$ or $m^{2}\equiv m_{x}^{2}$ , as appropriate. We additionally impose the boundary condition $g(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k)\to 0$ as $\rho\to\pm\infty$ , which gives the standard asymptotic behavior $g\sim e^{\mp\Delta\rho}$ .1717 17 Eq. (4.3) reduces to $[e^{\mp\rho}\frac{d}{d\rho}\left(e^{\pm\rho}\frac{d}{d\rho}\right)-m^{2}\rvert_{\rho\to\pm\infty}]g=0$ in the regime $\rho\to\pm\infty$ . We also note the symmetries of $g$ : $g(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k)=g(\rho^{\prime},\rho;k)=g(-\rho,-\rho^{\prime};k)=g(\rho,\rho^{\prime};-k)$ . These properties follow from (4.3) and/or the discussion after (3.32). It follows that $G$ only depends on $\tau$ and $\tau^{\prime}$ through the combination $|\tau-\tau^{\prime}|$ .

The equation for $g(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k)$ simplifies if we change variables from $\rho$ to the compactified coordinate

$$ \displaystyle r\equiv\int_{0}^{\rho}\frac{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}d\rho^{\prime}}{\sqrt{\cosh^{2}{\rho^{\prime}}-c^{2}}}=-i\mathbb{F}\left(i\rho\Big\rvert\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}\right), $$

where $\mathbb{F}(x|m)$ is the incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind. Equivalently, $\cosh{\rho}=\text{cn}\left(ir|\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}\right)$ , where $\text{cn}(x|m)$ is the Jacobi elliptic function.1818 18 Using (A.23), we can put the elliptic function in the form $\text{cn}\left(ir|\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}\right)=\text{dc}(r/\sqrt{1-c^{2}}|c^{2})$ , which makes it clearer that $\rho\mapsto r$ is a real map. The asymptotic behavior of $r$ as $\rho\to\pm\infty$ will play an important role in what follows. It is given by

$$ \displaystyle r \displaystyle\sim\pm\left(r_{m}+\bar{r}_{m}e^{\mp\rho}+O(e^{\mp 2\rho})\right), \displaystyle\text{where }r_{m}\equiv\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\mathbb{K}(c^{2})\text{ and }\bar{r}_{m}\equiv-2\sqrt{1-c^{2}}. $$

Note that the change of variables in (4.4) is essentially the one that puts the induced metric (3.16) in the conformal gauge form (up to rescaling by a constant factor).1919 19 See Appendix E of [50] for the form of the solution in conformal gauge.

After the change of variables, (4.3) becomes

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{d^{2}}{dr^{2}}-\frac{k^{2}}{1-c^{2}}-\frac{\sqrt{\cosh^{2}{\rho}-c^{2}}\sqrt{\gamma}m^{2}}{1-c^{2}}\biggr\rvert_{\cosh{\rho}\to\text{cn}\left(ir|\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}\right)}\right)g(r,r^{\prime};k) \displaystyle=-\frac{\delta(r-r^{\prime})}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}. $$

The solution to (4.6) may be written in the following piece-wise form:

$$ \displaystyle g(r,r^{\prime};k)\equiv a(k)\left[g^{R}(r;k)g^{L}(r^{\prime};k)\theta(r-r^{\prime})+g^{L}(r;k)g^{R}(r^{\prime};k)\theta(r^{\prime}-r)\right]. $$

Here, $g^{L}$ and $g^{R}$ solve (4.6) without the delta source term and satisfy the boundary conditions $g^{R}\to 0$ as $r\to r_{m}$ and $g^{L}\to 0$ as $r\to-r_{m}$ . The normalization $a(k)$ is fixed by needing to reproduce the prefactor of the delta function in (4.6):2020 20 Note that $a(k)$ is independent of $r$ , since $\frac{d}{dr}a(k)^{-1}=0$ because of (4.9)-(4.10). Furthermore, there is a “gauge” freedom to rescale $g^{R}$ or $g^{L}$ by some $\lambda\neq 0$ because we impose a single homogeneous boundary condition on these solutions. Because $a(k)$ is rescaled by a compensating factor of $1/\lambda$ , $g(r,r^{\prime};k)$ is unaffected.

$$ \displaystyle a(k) \displaystyle\equiv-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}\left(\frac{dg^{R}(r;k)}{dr}g^{L}(r;k)-\frac{dg^{L}(r;k)}{dr}g^{R}(r;k)\right)^{-1}. $$

The explicit forms of the homogeneous differential equations that $g^{L}$ and $g^{R}$ solve for the two different fluctuation modes are:

$$ \displaystyle\left(-\frac{d^{2}}{dr^{2}}+\frac{2c^{2}}{1-c^{2}}\text{cn}\left(ir|\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}\right)^{-2}\right)g^{L/R}_{yy}(r;k) \displaystyle=\frac{c^{2}-k^{2}}{1-c^{2}}g_{yy}^{L/R}(r;k), \displaystyle\left(-\frac{d^{2}}{dr^{2}}+\frac{2}{1-c^{2}}\text{cn}\left(ir|\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}\right)^{2}\right)g^{L/R}_{xx}(r;k) \displaystyle=\frac{c^{2}-k^{2}}{1-c^{2}}g_{xx}^{L/R}(r;k). $$

We can always choose $g^{L}$ and $g^{R}$ to satisfy

$$ \displaystyle g^{R}(r;k)=g^{R}(r;-k)=g^{L}(-r;k). $$

The second equality can be imposed because the masses are even under $\rho\to-\rho$ or, equivalently, $\text{cn}(ir|\frac{1}{1-c^{2}})$ is even under $r\to-r$ . Finally, we note that the boundary conditions impose the following asymptotic behavior:

$$ \displaystyle g^{R}\sim(r-r_{m})^{\Delta}\hskip 14.22636pt\text{as }r\to r_{m}, \displaystyle g^{L}\sim(r+r_{m})^{\Delta}\hskip 14.22636pt\text{as }r\to-r_{m}. $$

Eq. (4.1) and (4.7) give an explicit integral representation for the $G_{xx}$ and $G_{yy}$ in terms of solutions to the ODEs in (4.9)-(4.10). The next step is to convert the integral in (4.1) into a sum of residues. First, we replace $\tau-\tau^{\prime}$ by $|\tau-\tau^{\prime}|$ in (4.1) (see the comment below (4.3)) and close the contour in the upper half-plane. There is no contribution from the arc at infinity because of the $e^{ik|\tau-\tau^{\prime}|}$ term as long as $\tau\neq\tau^{\prime}$ . Next, we note that $g(r,r^{\prime};k)$ has poles where $1/a(k)$ , the Wronskian of $g^{R}(r;k)$ and $g^{L}(r;k)$ , is zero. For these values of $k$ , $g^{R}$ and $g^{L}$ are linearly dependent and define a single solution that vanishes at both $r=r_{m}$ and $r=-r_{m}$ . Eqs. (4.9) and (4.10) take the form of the time-independent Schrödinger equation with real potentials $V_{y}(r)\equiv\frac{2c^{2}}{1-c^{2}}\text{cn}\left(ir\rvert\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}\right)^{-2}$ and $V_{x}(r)\equiv\frac{2}{1-c^{2}}\text{cn}\left(ir\rvert\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}\right)^{2}$ (and $\hbar^{2}/2/m=1$ ). Therefore, the solutions $g^{L}\propto g^{R}$ at the poles are naturally interpreted as bound states of a one-dimensional particle with energy $\mathcal{E}=\frac{c^{2}-k^{2}}{1-c^{2}}$ moving in a potential $V(r)$ ( $\equiv V_{y}(r),V_{x}(r)$ ) with hard walls at $r=\pm r_{m}$ (because of the boundary conditions on $g^{R}$ and $g^{L}$ ). As we will verify explicitly in Sections 4.2 and 4.3, the poles of both $g_{yy}(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k)$ and $g_{xx}(\rho,\rho^{\prime};k)$ lie on the imaginary $k$ axis. Alternatively, this follows from the fact that the energy eigenvalues are necessarily real2121 21 The operator $-\frac{d^{2}}{dr^{2}}+V(r)$ is Hermitian with respect to the $L^{2}$ norm on the interval $[-r_{m},r_{m}]$ . and obey the bound $\mathcal{E}>\frac{c^{2}}{1-c^{2}}$ , which means the bound states only exist for $k^{2}<0$ . The lower bound on $\mathcal{E}$ is obvious for $V_{x}(r)$ , which attains the minimum value $\frac{2}{1-c^{2}}$ at $r=0$ , and can be verified numerically for $V_{y}(r)$ . The behavior of $g^{R}$ and $g^{L}$ at and away from the poles of $g(r,r;k)$ is illustrated in Figure 5.

Therefore, labelling the poles $k_{n}\in i\mathbb{R}^{+}$ , $n=0,1,2,\ldots$ , we can write the bulk-to-bulk propagator as

$$ \displaystyle G(r,\tau;r^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{ik_{n}|\tau-\tau^{\prime}|}\left(\frac{1}{4\pi g}\oint_{k_{n}}dk\text{ }a(k)\right)g^{R}(r;k_{n})g^{L}(r^{\prime};k_{n}). $$

We used (4.7) and the fact that $g^{R}(r;k_{n})g^{L}(r^{\prime};k_{n})=g^{L}(r;k_{n})g^{R}(r^{\prime};k_{n})$ , which follows because $g^{L}\propto g^{R}$ at $k=k_{n}$ . We have also assumed that the $k_{n}$ are simple poles of $g(r,r^{\prime};k)$ , so we can evaluate $g^{R}$ and $g^{L}$ at $k_{n}$ and pull them out of the contour integral.

To convert the series for the bulk-to-bulk propagator into a series for the boundary-to-boundary propagator, we send $\rho\to\eta_{1}\infty$ and $\rho^{\prime}\to\eta_{2}\infty$ (which sends $r\to\eta_{1}r_{m}$ and $r^{\prime}\to\eta_{2}r_{m}$ ) in accordance with (3.41). We can do so term-by-term in the series because each $g^{R}(r;k_{n})$ or $g^{L}(r;k_{n})$ vanishes at both $r=\pm r_{m}$ and combines with the divergent factor $e^{\eta\Delta\rho}$ to yield a finite result in terms of $k_{n}$ . There are two distinct cases to consider: $\eta_{1}=\eta_{2}$ , when the two bulk points approach the same boundary, and $\eta_{1}=-\eta_{2}$ , when the two bulk points approach opposite boundaries. These two cases are related in a simple way, as we can see by again exploiting the analogy with the Schrödinger equation in one dimension. Because the parities of the energy eigenstates in an even potential alternate (with the ground state being even), it follows that $g^{R}(r;k_{n})=g^{L}(-r;k_{n})=(-1)^{n}g^{R}(-r;k_{n})$ . Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\rho\to\eta\infty}e^{\eta\Delta\rho}g^{R}(r(\rho);k_{n})=\lim_{\rho\to-\eta\infty}e^{-\eta\Delta\rho}g^{L}(r(\rho);k_{n})=\eta^{n}\lim_{\rho\to\infty}e^{\Delta\rho}g^{R}(r(\rho);k_{n}). $$

This is useful because it is easier in practice to evaluate the first limit on the LHS of (4.14) when $\eta=1$ . This is because the limit of $e^{\Delta\rho}g^{R}(r(\rho);k)$ as $\rho\to\infty$ is finite for any $k$ while the limit as $\rho\to-\infty$ is finite only if $k=k_{n}$ .

Combining (3.41) and (4.13), and applying (3.42) and (4.14), we finally arrive at the following series representation for the boundary-to-boundary propagator:

$$ \displaystyle W(t_{1},t_{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{(2\Delta-1)^{2}}{2^{2\Delta-2}}\frac{g}{t_{12}^{2\Delta}}\frac{\chi^{2\Delta}}{|1-\chi|^{\Delta}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\biggr[(-\eta_{1}\eta_{2})^{n}e^{ik_{n}|\log|1-\chi||} \displaystyle\hskip 170.71652pt\times\left(\frac{1}{4\pi}\oint_{k_{n}}dka(k)\right)\left(\lim_{\rho\to\infty}e^{\Delta\rho}g^{R}(r(\rho);k_{n})\right)^{2}\biggr]. $$

Note that $\eta_{1}\eta_{2}=\text{sgn}(1-\chi)$ .

It is also possible to send the bulk points to the boundary without writing the Fourier integral as a sum of residues. This is mainly useful if we can interchange the limit and the integral, which requires that the two bulk points be sent to opposite boundaries. For instance, if we first send $\rho\to\infty$ inside the integrand of (4.1), then the step function in (4.7) sets $g(r,r^{\prime};k)=a(k)g^{R}(r;k)g^{L}(r^{\prime};k)$ and we must subsequently send $\rho^{\prime}\to-\infty$ because $g^{L}(r^{\prime};k)$ does not vanish at $\rho^{\prime}\to\infty$ for real $k$ . We find the following integral representation for the boundary-to-boundary propagator, which is valid when $\chi>1$ :

$$ \displaystyle W(t_{1},t_{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{(2\Delta-1)^{2}}{2^{2\Delta}\pi}\frac{g}{t_{12}^{2\Delta}}\frac{\chi^{2\Delta}}{(\chi-1)^{\Delta}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dke^{ik\log(\chi-1)}a(k)\left(\lim_{\rho\to\infty}e^{\Delta\rho}g^{R}(r(\rho);k)\right)^{2}. $$

In certain cases, this representation is more useful than (4.15).

### 4.2 Computing $W_{yy}$ , $W_{\theta\theta}$ and $W_{\phi\theta}$

We now implement the analysis developed in the previous section to find the boundary-to-boundary propagator $W_{yy}$ . Via (3.39) and (2.19), this determines the leading large charge behavior of the defect correlator $\braket{\Phi\Phi Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}/\braket{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}$ and of $G_{1}(\chi)$ . Using the superconformal Ward identities, we will then also determine $G_{Z\bar{Z}}(\chi)$ and $G_{\bar{Z}Z}(\chi)$ , which are equivalent to $W_{\theta\theta}$ and $W_{\phi\theta}$ .

#### 4.2.1 Computing $W_{yy}$

The key to computing $W_{yy}$ analytically is to recognize that (4.9) can be put in the Jacobi form of the Lamé differential equation. This ODE appeared previously in studies of one-loop corrections to the energies of “elliptic” classical strings in AdS ${}_{5}\times S^{5}$ [62, 63, 64, 65].2222 22 These are strings whose solutions can be written simply in terms of the Jacobi elliptic functions, and include the rotating folded string [62], pulsating strings [63], the string incident on anti-parallel lines on the boundary [64], and a two-parameter family of strings incident on contours that interpolate between a circle and antiparallel lines [65]. We summarize the equation in Appendix A along with conventions and identities for the elliptic integrals, Jacobi elliptic functions, and the theta functions. These special functions appear prominently throughout this section.

In order to put (4.9) into the Jacobi form of the Lamé equation, we rewrite it in terms of the new coordinate

$$ \displaystyle\sigma \displaystyle\equiv\frac{cr}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}+\mathbb{K}\left(\frac{1}{c^{2}}\right)+i\mathbb{K}\left(1-\frac{1}{c^{2}}\right). $$

Using the identities in (A.18)-(A.20) and (A.21)-(A.23), we can simplify (4.9) to

$$ \displaystyle\left[-\partial_{\sigma}^{2}+\frac{2}{c^{2}}\text{sn}^{2}\left(\sigma|\frac{1}{c^{2}}\right)\right]g_{yy}^{R/L}(\sigma;k) \displaystyle=\left(1-\frac{k^{2}}{c^{2}}\right)g^{R/L}_{yy}(\sigma;k). $$

This matches the form of the Lamé equation given in (A.29), if we identify the parameter $m$ and the eigenvalue $\Lambda$ to be:

$$ \displaystyle m \displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{c^{2}}, \displaystyle\Lambda \displaystyle\equiv 1-\frac{k^{2}}{c^{2}}. $$

Because they are ubiquitous in the following discussion, it is convenient to introduce the following standard shorthand:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{K} \displaystyle\equiv\mathbb{K}\left(\frac{1}{c^{2}}\right)=c\mathbb{K}(c^{2})-ic\mathbb{K}(1-c^{2}), \displaystyle\mathbb{K}^{\prime} \displaystyle\equiv\mathbb{K}\left(1-\frac{1}{c^{2}}\right)=c\mathbb{K}(1-c^{2}). $$

The second way of writing $\mathbb{K}$ and $\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ follows from (A.3)-(A.4). Since $\mathbb{K}(c^{2})$ and $\mathbb{K}(1-c^{2})$ are positive real numbers for $c^{2}\in(0,1)$ , it follows that $\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ and $\mathbb{K}+i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ are also positive real numbers, but $\mathbb{K}$ is complex. It will be convenient to work with $\mathbb{K}$ and $\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ and convert to explicitly real expressions only at the end.

We also note that as $r$ runs from $-r_{m}$ to $r_{m}$ , $\sigma$ in (4.17) runs from $\sigma_{-}$ to $\sigma_{+}$ along the real axis, where

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{-} \displaystyle\equiv 0, \displaystyle\sigma_{+} \displaystyle\equiv 2\mathbb{K}+2i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}. $$

As reviewed in Appendix A, the solutions to the Lamé equation are known in terms of theta functions. In particular, two linearly independent solutions to (4.18) are

$$ \displaystyle f^{\pm}(\sigma;\alpha)\equiv\frac{H(\pm\sigma+\alpha|m)}{\Theta(\sigma|m)}e^{\mp\sigma Z(\alpha|m)}. $$

Here $H$ , $\Theta$ and $Z$ are defined in (A.32), and $\alpha$ is related to $k$ by the transformation $\text{sn}\left(\alpha\bigr\rvert m\right)=\sqrt{1+k^{2}}$ or, equivalently,

$$ \displaystyle k\equiv i\text{cn}\left(\alpha\rvert m\right). $$

Because the Jacobi elliptic functions are doubly periodic (see (A.11)), the $\alpha$ complex plane is an infinite cover of the $k$ complex plane. We will see that this means the argument in Section 4.1 allowing us to convert the integral representation of the boundary-to-boundary propagator into a series representation can essentially be replicated in the $\alpha$ plane, but with some modification.2323 23 One could in principle work entirely in the $k$ plane instead, but it is more convenient to write the intermediate expressions for the bulk-to-bulk propagators using $\alpha$ and the Jacobi theta functions and then convert to expressions for the boundary-to-boundary propagators involving $k$ only at the end. We will take the “fundamental unit cell” in the $\alpha$ plane to be the rectangle with vertices at $\alpha=0$ , $\alpha=2\mathbb{K}+2i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ , $\alpha=-2i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ and $\alpha=2\mathbb{K}$ . A representative set of vertical and horizontal lines in the unit cell is depicted in Figure 6 a, and its image in the $k$ plane is depicted in Figure 6 b. The periodic placement of the other copies of the unit cell in the $\alpha$ plane is shown in Figure 7. In particular, it will be useful to note the pre-images of the real and positive imaginary axes of the $k$ plane in the $\alpha$ unit cell: As $k$ runs from $-\infty$ to $\infty$ along the real axis (see Figure 7 b), $\alpha$ runs along the line segment from $-i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ to $i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}+2\mathbb{K}$ (see Figure 7 a), and as $k$ runs from $0$ to $ci$ to $i$ to $i\infty$ along the imaginary axis (see Figure 7 b), $\alpha$ runs along the line segments from $\mathbb{K}$ to $\mathbb{K}+i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ to $0$ to $-i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ (see Figure 7 a).

Using (4.23), $g_{yy}^{R/L}$ can be written

$$ \displaystyle g_{yy}^{R}(\sigma;\alpha) \displaystyle=\frac{f^{+}(\sigma;\alpha)}{f^{+}(\sigma_{+};\alpha)}-\frac{f^{-}(\sigma;\alpha)}{f^{-}(\sigma_{+};\alpha)}, \displaystyle g_{yy}^{L}(\sigma;\alpha) \displaystyle=\frac{f^{-}(\sigma;\alpha)}{f^{-}(\sigma_{-};\alpha)}-\frac{f^{+}(\sigma;\alpha)}{f^{+}(\sigma_{-};\alpha)}. $$

These manifestly satisfy the boundary conditions $g_{yy}^{R}(\sigma_{+};\alpha)=g_{yy}^{L}(\sigma_{-};\alpha)=0$ . The parity and quasi-periodicity of the theta functions also imply that $g^{R/L}_{yy}(\sigma;\alpha)=g^{L/R}_{yy}(\sigma_{+}-\sigma;\alpha)$ and $g^{L/R}_{yy}(\sigma;\alpha+2\mathbb{K}a+2i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}b)=g^{L/R}_{yy}(\sigma;\alpha)$ , for $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ , which are analogous to (4.11).

Next, we compute the boundary limits of $g_{yy}^{R}(\sigma;\alpha)$ and $g_{yy}^{L}(\sigma;\alpha)$ . First, we note the behavior of $\sigma$ near the end points, which follows from (4.5) and (4.17):

$$ \displaystyle\sigma \displaystyle\sim\sigma_{\pm}\mp 2ce^{\mp\rho}, \displaystyle\text{ as }\rho \displaystyle\to\pm\infty. $$

Second, (4.12) implies that $g^{R}_{yy}\sim\sigma_{+}-\sigma$ as $\sigma\to\sigma_{+}$ and $g^{L}_{yy}\sim\sigma-\sigma_{-}$ as $\sigma\to\sigma_{-}$ (up to multiplicative factors independent of $\sigma$ ). Thus, we find:

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\rho\to\infty}e^{\rho}g_{yy}^{R}(\sigma;\alpha) \displaystyle=\lim_{\rho\to-\infty}e^{-\rho}g_{yy}^{L}(\sigma;\alpha)=-2c\frac{dg^{R}_{yy}}{d\sigma}\biggr\rvert_{\sigma=\sigma_{+}}=-4c(V(\alpha|m)-Z(\alpha|m)). $$

Here, $V(u|m)$ is defined in (A.33). Furthermore, the normalization becomes

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{a_{yy}(\alpha)} \displaystyle=-c\frac{dg_{yy}^{R}(\sigma_{+};\alpha)}{d\sigma}g_{yy}^{L}(\sigma_{+};\alpha)=4c(V(\alpha|m)-Z(\alpha|m))\sinh\left(\frac{\pi i\alpha}{\mathbb{K}}+\sigma_{+}Z(\alpha|m)\right). $$

To simplify this result, we used the fact that $a_{yy}(\alpha)$ is independent of $\sigma$ to evaluate the Wronskian at $\sigma=\sigma_{+}$ , a point at which $g_{yy}^{R}=0$ and $\frac{dg_{yy}^{R}}{d\sigma}$ is given by (4.28).

Using $\frac{dk}{d\alpha}=-i\text{sn}\left(\alpha|m\right)\text{dn}\left(\alpha|m\right)$ (note (4.24) and (A.14)) and (A.38) to express $V(\alpha|m)-Z(\alpha|m)$ in terms of the Jacobi elliptic functions, we can write the boundary limit of the bulk-to-bulk propagator as the following integral:

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\to\infty\\
\rho^{\prime}\to-\infty\end{subarray}}e^{\rho-\rho^{\prime}}G_{yy}(\rho,\tau;\rho^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})=-\frac{ci}{\pi g}\int_{-i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}}^{i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}+2\mathbb{K}}d\alpha\frac{\text{cn}\left(\alpha|m\right)\text{dn}^{2}\left(\alpha|m\right)\text{exp}\left(-\text{cn}\left(\alpha|m\right)|\tau-\tau^{\prime}|\right)}{\sinh\left(F(\alpha)\right)}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle F(\alpha)\equiv\frac{\pi i\alpha}{\mathbb{K}}+2(\mathbb{K}+i\mathbb{K}^{\prime})Z(\alpha|m). $$

This is equivalent to (4.16) except we changed the integration variable from $k$ to $\alpha$ .

The next step is to close the integration contour and pick up the residues at the poles. The integration contour in the $k$ plane can be closed using an arc at infinity, as in Figure 8 d, but the lifted contour in the $\alpha$ plane, shown in Figure 8 a, is not closed. However, the periodicity of the map from $\alpha$ to $k$ , illustrated in Figure 7, allows us to close the lifted contour as in Figure 8 b at the cost of doubling the value of the integral. In particular, the contribution from the top horizontal segment duplicates the contribution from the bottom horizontal segment, while the contributions from the right and left vertical segments cancel. One can also see that the integral over the closed contour in the $\alpha$ plane is twice the original integral by noting the image of the the closed contour in the $k$ plane, which is given in Figure 8 e.

To complete the argument, we need to identify the poles of the integrand of (4.30) that lie inside the closed contour. The poles of $\text{cn}(\alpha|m)$ and $\text{dn}(\alpha|m)$ , which are at $\alpha=i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}+2a\mathbb{K}+2bi\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ , $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ , all lie outside the contour. Thus, the only poles that contribute are the zeros of $\sinh\left(F(\alpha)\right)$ located inside the contour, which lie on the imaginary axis between $-i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ and $i\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ . We denote them $\alpha_{n}$ , $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ , and they satisfy2424 24 More generally, $\sinh\left(F(\alpha)\right)$ has zeros at $\alpha=\alpha_{n}+2a\mathbb{K}+2bi\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ , $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ .

$$ \displaystyle F(\alpha_{n})=n\pi i. $$

Because $Z(z|m)$ is odd, $\alpha_{0}=0$ and $\alpha_{-n}=-\alpha_{n}$ .

The result of deforming the contour to individually encircle the poles at each $\alpha_{n}$ is depicted in Figure 8 c, and its image in the $k$ plane is depicted in Figure 8 f. Note that each pole in Figure 8 c is encircled once while each pole in Figure 8 f is encircled twice. This is because $\alpha_{n}$ and $\alpha_{-n}$ for $n>0$ are mapped to the same point in the $k$ plane, so the contours individually encircling the two poles in the $\alpha$ plane are mapped to two contours encircling the same pole in the $k$ plane. Meanwhile, the pole at $\alpha_{0}=0$ is special: because the map in (4.24) is even and therefore identifies points positioned antipodally with respect to the origin in the $\alpha$ plane, the image of the closed loop encircling $\alpha=0$ with winding number $1$ is a closed loop encircling $k=i$ with winding number $2$ .

In order to evaluate the residues of (4.30) at $\alpha_{n}$ , it is convenient to note the following elementary result: If $f(z)$ and $g(z)$ are analytic at $z_{n}$ , $f(z_{n})=n\pi i$ , and $f^{\prime}(z_{n})\neq 0$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{z_{n}}dz\text{ }\frac{g(z)}{\sinh\left(f(z)\right)} \displaystyle=(-1)^{n}\frac{g(z_{n})}{f^{\prime}(z_{n})}. $$

Applying this result, we find that (4.30) can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\to\infty\\
\rho^{\prime}\to-\infty\end{subarray}}e^{\rho-\rho^{\prime}}G(\rho,\tau;\rho^{\prime},\tau^{\prime}) \displaystyle=\frac{c}{g}\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\frac{\text{cn}\left(\alpha_{n}|m\right)\text{dn}^{2}\left(\alpha_{n}|m\right)\text{exp}\left(-\text{cn}\left(\alpha_{n}|m\right)|\tau-\tau^{\prime}|\right)}{F^{\prime}(\alpha_{n})}. $$

Conveniently, the identity (A.37) lets us write the derivative of $Z(\alpha|m)$ , and therefore $F^{\prime}(\alpha)$ , in terms of the Jacobi elliptic functions. Additionally, we can use (A.3)-(A.6) and (A.7) to express $\mathbb{K}$ , $\mathbb{K}^{\prime}$ , $\mathbb{E}(\frac{1}{c^{2}})$ in terms of $\mathbb{K}(c^{2})$ and $\mathbb{E}(c^{2})$ , and we ultimately find

$$ \displaystyle F^{\prime}(\alpha)=\frac{2}{c}\left((1-c^{2})\mathbb{K}(c^{2})-\mathbb{E}(c^{2})\right)+2c\mathbb{K}(c^{2})\text{dn}^{2}\left(\alpha|m\right). $$

Eq. (4.30) is the final integral representation and (4.35), supplemented with (4.32), is the final series representation for the boundary limit of $G_{yy}$ expressed in terms of the $\alpha$ variables. Both expressions are perhaps more transparent when written in terms of the original $k$ variables, which gets rid of the elliptic functions and recasts the quantization condition in (4.32) in a more friendly form.

We first rewrite (4.30). $F$ can be written as a function of $k$ using $F(k)=\pi i+\int_{0}^{k}dk\frac{d\alpha}{dk}F^{\prime}(\alpha)$ , and noting (4.35). Furthermore, using (4.24) and the identities in (A.16)-(A.17), all of the elliptic functions can be expressed in terms of $k$ . Ultimately, we find

$$ \displaystyle W_{yy}(t_{1},t_{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{g}{\pi}\frac{1}{t_{12}^{2}}\frac{\chi^{2}}{\chi-1}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dk\frac{k\sqrt{1-c^{2}+k^{2}}\cos(k\log(\chi-1))}{\sqrt{1+k^{2}}\sinh\left(2\int_{0}^{k}d\ell\frac{\mathbb{K}(c^{2})\ell^{2}+\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}{\sqrt{1+\ell^{2}}\sqrt{1-c^{2}+\ell^{2}}}\right)}. $$

We used (3.41) to relate $W_{yy}$ to the boundary limit of $G_{yy}$ . Eq. (4.36) is valid when $\chi>1$ .

Next, we rewrite (4.34). We introduce the “fluctuation energies”:

$$ \displaystyle E_{n}\equiv-ik_{n}\equiv\text{cn}\left(\alpha_{n}\rvert m\right), $$

which are defined implicitly via (4.32). Note that $E_{0}=1$ and $E_{-n}=E_{n}$ . It is perhaps more illuminating to define the energies in terms of an integral quantization condition, which follows from writing (4.32) as $n\pi i=\int_{0}^{\alpha_{n}}d\alpha F^{\prime}(\alpha)=\int_{1}^{E_{n}}dE^{\prime}\frac{d\alpha}{dE^{\prime}}F^{\prime}(\alpha)$ and using (4.35) and the Jacobi elliptic function identities in (A.16)-(A.17) to simplify the result. This leads precisely to (2.27).

Again using (A.16)-(A.17) to express the elliptic functions in (4.34) in terms of $E_{n}$ , we find that the boundary-to-boundary propagator finally reduces to:

$$ \displaystyle W_{yy}(t_{1},t_{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{2g}{\pi}\frac{1}{t_{12}^{2}}\frac{\chi^{2}}{|1-\chi|}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\text{sgn}(1-\chi)^{n}f(E_{n})e^{-E_{n}|\log|1-\chi||}, $$

where $f(E)$ is given in (2.29). In (4.38), we have replaced $(-1)^{n}$ in (4.34) by $\text{sgn}(1-\chi)^{n}$ in accordance with the discussion around (4.14)-(4.15). Thus, the series representation in (4.38) is valid for both $\chi>1$ and $\chi<1$ . Finally, $G_{1}(\chi)=\frac{\pi}{2g}t_{12}^{2}W_{yy}(t_{1},t_{2})$ leads to (2.30).

#### Remarks about $G_{1}(\chi)$ .

Let us make a few remarks about the final result for $G_{1}(\chi)$ . Firstly, because $E_{n}=E_{-n}$ , the positive and negative terms in (4.38) can naturally be combined. In general, the $n=0$ term must be treated separately from the $n\geq 1$ terms. It is special both because $E_{0}=1$ is independent of $c^{2}$ (this corresponds to the fact that the lowest operator in the conformal block expansion of the scalar four-point functions is protected), and because $k_{0}$ is the only pole in the $k$ upper half plane that is mapped $1$ -to- $1$ with its pre-image $\alpha_{0}$ in the $\alpha$ plane.

Secondly, as a test of our results, we can consider the behavior of the four-point functions when $c^{2}=J=0$ , in which case there are no large charges on the Wilson line and the four-point functions reduce to two-point functions. (Likewise the classical string does not rotate in $S^{5}$ and the propagators for the $S^{5}$ and AdS5 modes reduce to those of scalars with $m^{2}=0$ and $m^{2}=2$ on AdS2). It follows in this case from (2.28) that $\rho(E)=1$ and $E_{n}=|n|+1$ , and from (2.29) that $f(1)=1$ and $f(E)=\frac{E}{2}$ for $E>1$ .2525 25 There is an order of limits issue when evaluating $f(E)$ at $E=1$ and $c^{2}=0$ . Namely, $\lim_{c\to 0}\lim_{E\to 1}f(E)=2\lim_{E\to 1}\lim_{c\to 0}f(E)=1$ . Since $E_{0}=1$ for all $c$ , the $n=0$ term in (4.38) is to be evaluated at $E=1$ before we take $c\to 0$ . Therefore, the series representation of $W_{yy}(t_{1},t_{2})$ from (4.38) becomes

$$ \displaystyle W_{yy}(t_{1},t_{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{2g}{\pi}\frac{1}{t_{12}^{2}}\frac{\chi^{2}}{|1-\chi|}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\text{sgn}(1-\chi)^{n}(n+1)e^{-(n+1)|\log|1-\chi||}. $$

Given that $4\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}ne^{-nx}=\sinh^{-2}{\frac{x}{2}}$ and $4\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}ne^{-nx}=\cosh^{-2}{\frac{x}{2}}$ , the series can be explicitly summed for any $\chi$ . We arrive at the result

$$ \displaystyle\braket{\Phi_{i}(t_{1})\Phi_{j}(t_{2})}=W_{yy}(t_{1},t_{2})\delta_{ij}=\frac{2g}{\pi}\frac{1}{t_{12}^{2}}\delta_{ij}. $$

This correctly reproduces the leading behavior of the scalar two-point function in (2.17).

Thirdly, (2.30) is a compact representation of a function defined piecewise on $\chi\in(-\infty,0)$ , $\chi\in(0,1)$ , $\chi\in(1,2)$ and $\chi\in(2,\infty)$ . Unpacking the absolute values yields

$$ \displaystyle G_{1}(\chi) \displaystyle=\theta(-\chi)G^{(-\infty,0)}_{1}(\chi)+\theta(\chi)\theta(1-\chi)G^{(0,1)}_{1}(\chi) \displaystyle+\theta(\chi-1)\theta(2-\chi)G^{(1,2)}_{1}(\chi)+\theta(\chi-2)G^{(2,\infty)}_{1}(\chi), $$

where $\theta(b-x)\theta(a-x)$ is $1$ if $a<x<b$ and $0$ otherwise and $G_{1}^{I}(\chi)$ denotes the series representation of $G_{1}(\chi)$ on the interval $I\subset\mathbb{R}$ . Explicitly, we have

$$ \displaystyle G^{(-\infty,0)}_{1}(\chi) \displaystyle=\chi^{2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\frac{f(E_{n})}{(1-\chi)^{E_{n}+1}}, \displaystyle G_{1}^{(0,1)}(\chi) \displaystyle=\chi^{2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f(E_{n})(1-\chi)^{E_{n}-1}, \displaystyle G_{1}^{(1,2)}(\chi) \displaystyle=\chi^{2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}(-1)^{n}f(E_{n})(\chi-1)^{E_{n}-1}, \displaystyle G_{1}^{(2,\infty)}(\chi) \displaystyle=\chi^{2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}(-1)^{n}\frac{f(E_{n})}{(\chi-1)^{E_{n}+1}}. $$

From the discussion around Figure 2, one would expect $G_{1}$ to behave piecewise on $\chi\in(-\infty,0)$ , $\chi\in(0,1)$ and $\chi\in(1,\infty)$ . The apparently special role of $\chi=2$ in (4.41) is an artifact of the series representation. In particular, while the series representations $G_{1}^{(1,2)}(\chi)$ and $G_{1}^{(2,\infty)}(\chi)$ do not converge at $\chi=2$ , the integral representation in (4.36) is perfectly smooth at $\chi=2$ .2626 26 This is analogous to the fact that $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^{n}$ diverges, whereas $\frac{1}{1-x}$ is perfectly smooth, at $x=-1$ . This is related to the convergence of the OPE as we will discuss shortly.

Finally, we comment on how (2.30) is consistent with $G_{1}(\chi)\to 1$ as $\chi\to 0$ , which is imposed by the OPE limit in which the two light operators (or the two heavy operators) approach each other (in this limit, the leading exchanged operator is the identity). As $\chi\to 0$ , the exponentially damping term in (2.30) is turned off and the series diverges due to the “infinite tail” consisting of terms with arbitrarily large values of $n$ . The contribution of the tail is captured by an integral over $E$ weighted by the energy density $\rho(E)$ . Since large values of $E$ dominate, we may replace the energy density and form factor by their asymptotic forms: $\rho(E)\sim\frac{2\mathbb{K}(c^{2})}{\pi}$ , $f(E)\sim\frac{\pi}{4}\frac{E}{\mathbb{K}(c^{2})}$ . Thus, as $\chi\to 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f(E_{n})e^{-E_{n}|\log(1-\chi)|} \displaystyle\sim\int_{E_{\rm cutoff}}^{\infty}2\rho(E)f(E)e^{-E|\chi|}dE\sim\int_{E_{\rm cutoff}}^{\infty}Ee^{-E|\chi|}dE\sim\frac{1}{\chi^{2}}, $$

where the leading behavior does not depend on the precise value of $E_{\rm cutoff}\gg 1$ . Eq. (4.44) combines with the prefactor $\chi^{2}/|1-\chi|\sim\chi^{2}$ in (2.30) to yield $G_{1}(\chi)\sim 1$ , as desired. The key input in this reasoning is the fact that $2\rho(E)f(E)\sim E$ asymptotically for large $E$ . Likewise, $G_{4}(\chi)\to 1$ follows from (2.31) and $2\rho(E)f(E)(E^{2}-1)/6\sim E^{3}/6$ asymptotically. Our argument is similar in spirit to the general analysis in [54] of how the consistency of the OPE in different channels constrains its large dimension asymptotics in a 1d CFT.

#### Convergence of the series representation.

The divergence of the series in (4.42)-(4.43) at $\chi=2$ can be understood in terms of the limited radius of convergence of the OPE in a CFT. We recall that the product of two operators $O_{1}(s_{1})$ and $O_{2}(s_{2})$ can be written as a convergent sum over primaries at a point $s$ only if there exists a sphere centered on $s$ that contains $O_{1}(s_{1})$ and $O_{2}(s_{2})$ and no other operators (see, e.g., [66, 67]). As we discuss in greater detail in Section 5, the series representations of $G_{1}(\chi)$ are essentially conformal block expansions of the four-point function in the light-heavy channel, expanded around the insertion point of the heavy operator. To illustrate concretely how this is related to (4.42)-(4.43), let us use the conformal symmetry to set $t_{1}=1$ , $t_{3}=0$ and $t_{4}=\infty$ , in which case $1-\chi=t_{2}$ . Then, $G_{1}^{(-\infty,0)}(\chi)$ and $G_{1}^{(2,\infty)}(\chi)$ are sums over positive powers of $1/t_{2}$ and correspond to taking the OPE of $\Phi(t_{2})$ with $\bar{Z}^{J}(\infty)$ centered at $\infty$ , while $G_{1}^{(0,1)}(\chi)$ and $G_{1}^{(1,2)}(\chi)$ are sums over positive powers of $t_{2}$ and correspond to taking the OPE of $\Phi(t_{2})$ with $Z^{J}(0)$ centered at $0$ . Note that a zero-sphere (i.e., two points) centered at $0$ and enclosing only $\Phi(t_{2})$ and $Z^{J}(0)$ exists only if $|t_{2}|<1$ because the sphere would otherwise also enclose $\Phi(1)$ . Likewise, a zero-sphere centered at $\infty$ and enclosing only $\Phi(t_{2})$ and $\bar{Z}^{J}(\infty)$ exists only if $|t_{2}|>1$ . Therefore the OPE is indeed expected to diverge at $t_{2}=1,-1$ or $\chi=0,2$ .

We can comment a little more concretely about the analyticity of the four-point functions and the convergence of their series representations. The convergence of each of the series in (4.42) and (4.43) is determined by the growth of $E_{n}$ with $n$ . For $c\in(0,1)$ , the energy density $\rho(E)$ is sharply peaked at $E=1$ and flattens out as $E$ increases. More precisely, $\rho(E)\sim\text{constant}/\sqrt{E-1}$ near $E=1$ 2727 27 Explicitly, $\rho(E)\sim\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\pi}\frac{\mathbb{K}(c^{2})-\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}{c}\frac{1}{\sqrt{E-1}}$ near $E=1$ . and $\rho(E)\sim\frac{2\mathbb{K}(c^{2})}{\pi}+O(1/E^{2})$ for large $E$ , from which it follows that $E_{n}\sim\frac{\pi}{2\mathbb{K}(c^{2})}|n|+O(|n|^{0})$ for large $|n|$ . The asymptotically linear growth of $E_{n}$ with $|n|$ means that each $G_{1}^{I}(\chi)$ converges absolutely and is analytic on a subset of the complex plane that includes the real interval $I$ .2828 28 Absolute convergence follows from the ratio test and analyticity follows from applying Morera’s theorem. Because the terms in the series consist of non-integer powers of $1-\chi$ , the series are multi-valued and the principal sheet should be defined with a branch cut. For example, $G_{1}^{(-\infty,0)}(\chi)$ converges for all $\chi\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $|\chi-1|>1$ with a natural choice of branch-cut being the interval $\chi\in(2,\infty)$ ; $G_{1}^{(2,\infty)}(\chi)$ converges for all $|\chi-1|>1$ with branch-cut $\chi\in(-\infty,0)$ ; $G_{1}^{(0,1)}(\chi)$ converges for all $0<|\chi-1|<1$ with branch-cut $\chi\in(1,2)$ ; and $G_{1}^{(1,2)}(\chi)$ converges for all $0<|\chi-1|<1$ with branch-cut $\chi\in(0,1)$ .

Each series in (4.42) and (4.43) can be analytically continued beyond its domain of convergence. In particular, the integral in (4.36) provides the maximal extension of $G^{(1,2)}_{1}$ and $G^{(2,\infty)}$ and smoothly stitches together their disjoint domains of convergence, which lie inside and outside the unit disk centered at $\chi=1$ . Meanwhile, the analytic continuation of $G_{1}^{(-\infty,0)}$ and $G_{1}^{(0,1)}$ yields two additional distinct multi-valued functions on the complex $\chi$ plane. These observations are in accordance with the general behavior discussed in Section 2.1. Similar comments apply to the series expressions for $G_{Z\bar{Z}}$ , $G_{\bar{Z}Z}$ and $G_{4}$ , which we turn to in Section 4.2.2 and 4.3.

#### 4.2.2 Computing $G_{Z\bar{Z}}$ and $G_{\bar{Z}Z}$ from $G_{1}$

Next, we determine integral and series representations of the defect four-point functions in (2.20)-(2.21), in which the light insertions are $Z$ and $\bar{Z}$ . According to (3.45)-(3.46), the leading contribution in the large charge expansion is given by the classical vertex operators in (3.47) and the first subleading correction is determined by the boundary-to-boundary propagators $W_{\theta\theta}$ and $W_{\theta\phi}$ . One could try to solve for these boundary-to-boundary propagators in the same way that we solved for $W_{yy}$ . This approach is more cumbersome for the $\theta$ and $\phi$ propagators than for the $y$ propagators— both because $m_{\theta\phi}^{2}$ is less simple than $m_{yy}^{2}$ and because the Green’s equations solved by $G_{\theta\theta}$ and $G_{\phi\theta}$ are coupled— but one can nonetheless make progress working perturbatively in small $c^{2}$ , as we demonstrate in Appendix C.

To determine the subleading corrections to $G_{Z\bar{Z}}(\chi)$ and $G_{\bar{Z}Z}(\chi)$ (which are equivalent to $W_{\theta\theta}$ and $W_{\theta\phi}$ ) for general $c^{2}$ , we will instead make use of the superconformal Ward identities. The general solutions to the first order differential equations (2.26) can be written as

$$ \displaystyle G_{2}(\chi) \displaystyle=\frac{\chi^{2}}{(1-\chi)^{2}}\left(C_{2}(\chi_{0})+\int_{\chi_{0}}^{\chi}dx\left(\frac{1}{x}-1\right)\frac{dG_{1}}{dx}\right), \displaystyle G_{3}(\chi) \displaystyle=\chi^{2}\left(C_{3}(\chi_{0})-\int_{\chi_{0}}^{\chi}dx\frac{1}{x}\frac{dG_{1}}{dx}\right). $$

After integrating by parts (with $C_{2}(\chi_{0})$ and $C_{3}(\chi_{0})$ absorbing the boundary terms) and converting from $G_{2},G_{3}$ to $G_{Z\bar{Z}},G_{\bar{Z}Z}$ using (2.23), this becomes:

$$ \displaystyle G_{Z\bar{Z}}(\chi) \displaystyle=\frac{\chi^{2}}{(1-\chi)^{2}}\left[C_{2}(\chi_{0})+\frac{1-\chi}{\chi^{2}}G_{1}(\chi)+\int_{\chi_{0}}^{\chi}dx\frac{G_{1}(x)}{x^{2}}\right], \displaystyle G_{\bar{Z}Z}(\chi) \displaystyle=\chi^{2}\left[C_{3}(\chi_{0})+\frac{1-\chi}{\chi^{2}}G_{1}(\chi)-\int_{\chi_{0}}^{\chi}dx\frac{G_{1}(x)}{x^{2}}\right]. $$

The remaining integrals in (4.47) and (4.48) are easy to evaluate when $G_{1}$ is expressed using the integral representation in (4.36) or the series representations in (4.42)-(4.43).

Let’s first determine the series representations of $G_{Z\bar{Z}}$ and $G_{\bar{Z}Z}$ . Because the series representations of $G_{1}$ are defined piecewise, we will likewise consider the four cases, $\chi\in(-\infty,0)$ , $(0,1)$ , $(1,2)$ and $(2,\infty)$ separately. We pick $\chi_{0}=\infty$ when $\chi\in(-\infty,0)$ or $\chi\in(2,\infty)$ and $\chi_{0}=1$ when $\chi\in(0,1)$ or $\chi\in(1,2)$ . Since $G_{1}(\chi)$ is finite as $\chi\to\infty$ or $\chi\to 1$ (see (4.42)-(4.43)), it follows that for these values of $\chi_{0}$ the integration constants can be written

$$ \displaystyle C_{2}(\chi_{0}) \displaystyle=\lim_{\chi\to\chi_{0}}\frac{(1-\chi)^{2}}{\chi^{2}}G_{Z\bar{Z}}, \displaystyle C_{3}(\chi_{0}) \displaystyle=\lim_{\chi\to\chi_{0}}\frac{1}{\chi^{2}}G_{\bar{Z}Z}. $$

Furthermore, the limits $\chi\to 1$ and $\chi\to\infty$ correspond to $Z$ and $\bar{Z}$ becoming coincident with $Z^{J}$ and $\bar{Z}^{J}$ in (2.20) and (2.21), which means that $C_{2}(\chi_{0})$ and $C_{3}(\chi_{0})$ can be expressed in terms of certain normalized OPE coefficients.

In particular, the primary of lowest conformal dimension in the OPE of $Z$ and $Z^{J}$ (resp. $\bar{Z}$ and $\bar{Z}^{J}$ ) is $Z^{J+1}$ ( $\bar{Z}^{J+1}$ ) and the primary of lowest conformal dimension in the OPE of $Z$ and $\bar{Z}^{J}$ ( $\bar{Z}$ and $Z^{J}$ ) is $Z^{J-1}$ ( $\bar{Z}^{J-1}$ ). Thus, the leading contributions to the OPE of $Z$ and $Z^{J}$ and of $\bar{Z}$ and $Z^{J}$ are

$$ \displaystyle Z(t)Z^{J}(t^{\prime}) \displaystyle\sim\frac{\mathcal{C}_{ZZ^{J}\bar{Z}^{J+1}}}{\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J+1}\bar{Z}^{J+1}}}Z^{J+1}(t^{\prime}), \displaystyle\bar{Z}(t)Z^{J}(t^{\prime}) \displaystyle\sim\frac{\mathcal{C}_{\bar{Z}Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J-1}}}{\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J-1}\bar{Z}^{J-1}}}\frac{1}{(t-t^{\prime})^{2}}Z^{J-1}(t^{\prime}) $$

as $t\to t^{\prime}$ , with subleading terms suppressed by positive powers of $t-t^{\prime}$ . The relations with $Z\leftrightarrow\bar{Z}$ similarly hold. Then, sending $t_{1}\to t_{3}$ and $t_{2}\to t_{4}$ , in which case $\chi\sim\frac{t_{34}^{2}}{t_{13}t_{24}}$ , or $t_{1}\to t_{4}$ and $t_{2}\to t_{3}$ , in which case $1-\chi\sim\frac{t_{14}t_{23}}{t_{34}^{2}}$ , in (2.20)-(2.21) and applying the OPEs in (4.50), we find the following four limiting values of $G_{Z\bar{Z}}$ and $G_{\bar{Z}Z}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\chi\to\infty}G_{Z\bar{Z}}(\chi) \displaystyle=\lim_{\chi\to 1}G_{\bar{Z}Z}(\chi) \displaystyle=\frac{\pi}{4g}\frac{\mathcal{C}_{ZZ^{J}\bar{Z}^{J+1}}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}Z^{J+1}}}{\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J+1}\bar{Z}^{J+1}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}}, \displaystyle\lim_{\chi\to\infty}\frac{G_{\bar{Z}Z}(\chi)}{\chi^{2}} \displaystyle=\lim_{\chi\to 1}(1-\chi)^{2}G_{Z\bar{Z}}(\chi) \displaystyle=\frac{\pi}{4g}\frac{\mathcal{C}_{\bar{Z}Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J-1}}\mathcal{C}_{Z\bar{Z}^{J}Z^{J-1}}}{\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J-1}\bar{Z}^{J-1}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}}. $$

Since the normalized OPE coefficient in (4.52) is equal to the one in (4.51) up to a unit shift in the large charge, it is useful to note that $c^{2}(J-1)=c^{2}(J)-\frac{dc^{2}(J)}{dJ}+O(1/g^{2})$ and $\frac{dc^{2}(J)}{dJ}=\frac{1-c^{2}}{2g\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}$ , which follows from (2.10). Meanwhile, the OPE coefficient in (4.51) was determined previously in [41] and is given in (2.12). Consequently, the constants of integration in (4.49) with $\chi_{0}=1$ and $\chi_{0}=\infty$ simplify to

$$ \displaystyle C_{2}(\infty) \displaystyle=C_{3}(1)=g\pi c^{2}+\frac{\pi}{2}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}, \displaystyle C_{2}(1) \displaystyle=C_{3}(\infty)=g\pi c^{2}. $$

Substituting the appropriate series expression for $G_{1}$ from (4.42)-(4.43) and (4.53) for $C_{2}$ and $C_{3}$ in (4.47)-(4.48) determines $G_{Z\bar{Z}}$ and $G_{\bar{Z}Z}$ for any $\chi$ . For $\chi\in(0,2)$ , we find

$$ \displaystyle G_{Z\bar{Z}}(\chi) \displaystyle=\frac{g\pi c^{2}\chi^{2}}{(1-\chi)^{2}}+\frac{\chi^{2}}{|1-\chi|}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\text{sgn}\left(1-\chi\right)^{n+1}f(E_{n})\frac{E_{n}-1}{E_{n}}e^{-(E_{n}-1)|\log|1-\chi||}, \displaystyle G_{\bar{Z}Z}(\chi) \displaystyle=\left(g\pi c^{2}+\frac{\pi}{2}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}\right)\chi^{2} \displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt+\frac{\chi^{2}}{|1-\chi|}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\text{sgn}\left(1-\chi\right)^{n+1}f(E_{n})\frac{E_{n}+1}{E_{n}}e^{-(E_{n}+1)|\log|1-\chi||}. $$

For $\chi\in(-\infty,0)\cup(2,\infty)$ , we find

$$ \displaystyle G_{Z\bar{Z}}(\chi) \displaystyle=\left(g\pi c^{2}+\frac{\pi}{2}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}\right)\frac{\chi^{2}}{(1-\chi)^{2}} \displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt+\frac{\chi^{2}}{|1-\chi|}\sum_{n}\text{sgn}\left(1-\chi\right)^{n+1}f(E_{n})\frac{E_{n}+1}{E_{n}}e^{-(E_{n}+1)|\log|1-\chi||}. \displaystyle G_{\bar{Z}Z}(\chi) \displaystyle=g\pi c^{2}\chi^{2}+\frac{\chi^{2}}{|1-\chi|}\sum_{n}\text{sgn}\left(1-\chi\right)^{n+1}f(E_{n})\frac{E_{n}-1}{E_{n}}e^{-(E_{n}-1)|\log|1-\chi||}, $$

One readily checks that (4.54)-(4.55) and (4.56)-(4.57) satisfy the crossing condition in (2.24).

We can also determine the integral representations of $G_{Z\bar{Z}}$ and $G_{\bar{Z}Z}$ by applying (4.47)-(4.48) and substituting (4.36) for $G_{1}(\chi)=\frac{\pi t_{12}^{2}}{2g}W_{yy}(t_{1},t_{2})$ . We find

$$ \displaystyle G_{Z\bar{Z}}(\chi) \displaystyle=\frac{\chi^{2}}{(1-\chi)^{2}}\biggr[g\pi c^{2}+\frac{\pi}{4}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})} \displaystyle+\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dk\frac{\sqrt{1-c^{2}+k^{2}}\left[-k\cos(k\log(\chi-1))+\sin(k\log(\chi-1))\right]}{2\sqrt{1+k^{2}}\sinh\left(2\int_{0}^{k}d\ell\frac{\mathbb{K}(c^{2})\ell^{2}+\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}{\sqrt{1+\ell^{2}}\sqrt{1-c^{2}+\ell^{2}}}\right)}\biggr], \displaystyle G_{\bar{Z}Z}(\chi) \displaystyle=\chi^{2}\biggr[g\pi c^{2}+\frac{\pi}{4}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})} \displaystyle+\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dk\frac{\sqrt{1-c^{2}+k^{2}}\left[-k\cos(k\log(\chi-1))-\sin(k\log(\chi-1))\right]}{2\sqrt{1+k^{2}}\sinh\left(2\int_{0}^{k}d\ell\frac{\mathbb{K}(c^{2})\ell^{2}+\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}{\sqrt{1+\ell^{2}}\sqrt{1-c^{2}+\ell^{2}}}\right)}\biggr]. $$

Because $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\cos(ak)f(k)dk\to 0$ as $a\to\pm\infty$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\sin(ak)}{k}f(k)\to\text{sgn}(a)\pi f(0)$ as $a\to\pm\infty$ for a smooth function $f(k)$ , the integrals in (4.58) and (4.59) approach $-\frac{\pi}{4}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}$ and $\frac{\pi}{4}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}$ as $\chi\to 1$ and approach $\frac{\pi}{4}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}$ and $-\frac{\pi}{4}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}$ as $\chi\to\infty$ , respectively. Therefore, (4.58) and (4.59) reproduce (4.51)-(4.52), as required by the OPE limit.

### 4.3 Computing $W_{xx}$

Finally, we implement the general analysis from Section 4.1 to find the boundary-to-boundary propagator $W_{xx}$ . Via (3.40) and (2.22), this determines the leading large charge behavior of defect correlators $\braket{\mathbb{D}\mathbb{D}Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}/\braket{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}$ or, equivalently, $G_{4}(\chi)$ . The computation of $W_{xx}$ is very similar to that of $W_{yy}$ . We will therefore suppress some of the details and will use tildes to distinguish between parallel quantities.

We begin by rewriting (4.10) in terms of the new variable $\tilde{\sigma}\equiv ir$ . Using the identity in (A.16) to simplify the result, we find:

$$ \displaystyle\left[-\partial_{\tilde{\sigma}}^{2}+\frac{2}{1-c^{2}}\text{sn}^{2}\left(\tilde{\sigma}|\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}\right)\right]g_{xx}^{R/L}(\tilde{\sigma};k) \displaystyle=\left(\frac{2+k^{2}-c^{2}}{1-c^{2}}\right)g^{R/L}_{xx}(\tilde{\sigma};k). $$

This is also in the Jacobi form of the Lamé equation given in (A.29) if we identify the parameter, $\tilde{m}$ , and the eigenvalue, $\tilde{\Lambda}$ , to be:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{m} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}, \displaystyle\tilde{\Lambda} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{2+k^{2}-c^{2}}{1-c^{2}}. $$

It is again useful to introduce the following shorthand:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\mathbb{K}} \displaystyle\equiv\mathbb{K}\left(\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}\right)=\sqrt{1-c^{2}}(\mathbb{K}(1-c^{2})-i\mathbb{K}(c^{2})), \displaystyle\tilde{\mathbb{K}}^{\prime} \displaystyle\equiv\mathbb{K}\left(\frac{c^{2}}{c^{2}-1}\right)=\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\mathbb{K}(c^{2}). $$

The second way of writing $\tilde{\mathbb{K}}$ and $\tilde{\mathbb{K}}^{\prime}$ follows from (A.3)-(A.4) and makes it clear that $\tilde{\mathbb{K}}^{\prime}$ and $\tilde{\mathbb{K}}+i\tilde{\mathbb{K}}^{\prime}$ are positive real numbers.

As the coordinate $r$ runs from $-r_{m}$ to $r_{m}$ , the coordinate $\tilde{\sigma}$ runs from $\tilde{\sigma}_{-}\equiv-i\tilde{\mathbb{K}}^{\prime}$ to $\tilde{\sigma}_{+}\equiv i\tilde{\mathbb{K}}^{\prime}$ along the imaginary axis. Its behavior near the end points follows from (4.5):

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\sigma} \displaystyle\sim\tilde{\sigma}_{\pm}\mp 2i\sqrt{1-c^{2}}e^{\mp\rho}, \displaystyle\text{as }\rho\to\pm\infty. $$

Having recognized (4.60) as the Jacobi form of the Lamé equation with the identification in (4.61), we identify two linearly independent solutions to be

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{f}_{\pm}(\tilde{\sigma};\tilde{\alpha})\equiv\frac{H(\pm\tilde{\sigma}+\tilde{\alpha}|\tilde{m})}{\Theta(\tilde{\sigma}|\tilde{m})}e^{\mp\tilde{\sigma}Z(\tilde{\alpha}|\tilde{m})}. $$

Here, $\tilde{\alpha}$ is related to $k$ by

$$ \displaystyle k\equiv-i\text{sn}\left(\tilde{\alpha}|\tilde{m}\right). $$

Because of the double-periodicity of $\text{sn}\left(\tilde{\alpha}|\tilde{m}\right)$ , the $\tilde{\alpha}$ -plane is an infinite cover of the $k$ plane. See Figure 9. We take the fundamental unit cell to be the rectangle with vertices at $\tilde{\alpha}=-\tilde{\mathbb{K}}-2i\tilde{\mathbb{K}}^{\prime}$ , $\tilde{\alpha}=-\tilde{\mathbb{K}}$ , $\tilde{\alpha}=\tilde{\mathbb{K}}+2i\tilde{\mathbb{K}}^{\prime}$ , and $\tilde{\alpha}=\tilde{\mathbb{K}}$ . Let us check that these indeed satisfy the boundary condition $g^{R}_{xx}(\tilde{\sigma},\tilde{\alpha})\to 0$ as $\tilde{\sigma}\to\tilde{\sigma}_{+}$ (and therefore also $g^{L}_{xx}(\tilde{\sigma},\tilde{\alpha})\to 0$ as $\tilde{\sigma}\to\tilde{\sigma}_{-}$ ). We note the behavior of $\Theta(\tilde{\sigma}|\tilde{m})$ near $\tilde{\sigma}=\tilde{\sigma}_{+}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Theta(\tilde{\sigma}|\tilde{m})=\frac{\pi}{2\tilde{\mathbb{K}}}\theta_{4}^{\prime}\left(\frac{\pi\tilde{\tau}}{2},\tilde{q}\right)(\tilde{\sigma}-\tilde{\sigma}_{+})+O(\tilde{\sigma}-\tilde{\sigma}_{+})^{2}, $$

where $\tilde{\tau}\equiv\frac{i\tilde{\mathbb{K}}^{\prime}}{\tilde{\mathbb{K}}}$ and $\tilde{q}\equiv e^{i\pi\tilde{\tau}}$ . Furthermore, $\Theta$ is related to $H$ after a translation by $\pm i\tilde{\mathbb{K}}^{\prime}$ :

This reproduces the expected behavior in (4.12).

Thus, sending $g_{xx}^{R}(\tilde{\sigma};\tilde{\alpha})$ and $g_{xx}^{L}(\tilde{\sigma};\tilde{\alpha})$ to opposite boundaries yields

Furthermore, the normalization can be simplified to

where we used the fact that $a_{xx}(\tilde{\alpha})$ is independent of $\tilde{\sigma}$ to evaluate the Wronskian at $\tilde{\sigma}=0$ .

Using $\frac{dk}{d\tilde{\alpha}}=-i\text{cn}\left(\tilde{\alpha}\rvert\tilde{m}\right)\text{dn}\left(\tilde{\alpha}\rvert\tilde{m}\right)$ (note (4.66) and (A.13)) and (A.36)-(A.38) to express various combinations of the theta functions in terms of the Jacobi elliptic functions, we may write the boundary limit of the bulk-to-bulk propagators as the following integral:2929 29 To simplify the factors independent of $\tilde{\alpha}$ in front of the integral, we used $i\frac{2\tilde{\mathbb{K}}}{\pi}\frac{\theta_{4}(0,\tilde{q})}{\theta_{4}^{\prime}(\frac{\pi\tilde{\tau}}{2},\tilde{q})}\tilde{q}^{-\frac{1}{4}}\tilde{m}^{\frac{1}{4}}=1$ , which can be deduced from various identities in Ch. 1 of [68].

#### Remarks about $G_{4}(\chi)$ .

Now we make two remarks about the final result for $G_{4}(\chi)$ . We can check that the four-point function reduces to the two-point function of the displacement operators when $c=0$ . In this case the series representation of $W_{xx}(t_{1},t_{2})$ from (4.83) becomes

$$ \displaystyle W_{xx}(t_{1},t_{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{2g}{\pi}\frac{1}{t_{12}^{4}}\frac{\chi^{4}}{(1-\chi)^{2}}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\text{sgn}(1-\chi)^{n+1}n(n+1)(n+2)e^{-(n+1)|\log|1-\chi||}. $$

Given that $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}n(n^{2}-1)e^{-nx}=\frac{3}{8}\sinh^{-4}{\frac{x}{2}}$ and $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}n(n^{2}-1)e^{-nx}=\frac{3}{8}\cosh^{-4}{\frac{x}{2}}$ , we can explicitly sum the series for $\chi>1$ and $\chi<1$ . In both cases, we arrive at the result

$$ \displaystyle\braket{\mathbb{D}_{a}(t_{1})\mathbb{D}_{b}(t_{2})} \displaystyle=W_{xx}(t_{1},t_{2})\delta_{ab}=\frac{12g}{\pi}\frac{1}{t_{12}^{4}}\delta_{ab}. $$

This reproduces the leading behavior of (2.17).

Next, comparing (4.36) and (4.82) or (4.38) and (4.83), one sees that $G_{1}$ and $G_{4}$ satisfy:

$$ \displaystyle G_{4}(\chi) \displaystyle=-\frac{\chi^{4}}{6}\left(3\frac{d}{d\chi}+(\chi-1)\frac{d^{2}}{d\chi^{2}}\right)\frac{G_{1}(\chi)}{\chi^{2}}. $$

This identity, in analogy with (2.26), should essentially be a Ward identity that relates the four-point functions in (2.13) and (2.14) that belong to the same superconformal multiplet.

## 5 Extracting OPE data from the four-point functions

In this section, we extract defect OPE data of operators with large charge from the four-point defect correlators in (2.13)-(2.14). The analysis in this case is particularly simple because the series representations of the defect correlators in (2.30)-(2.31) and (4.54)-(4.57) are already essentially in the form of conformal block expansions, and because the conformal blocks simplify when some of the operators have large dimensions. For a given four-point function, each term in the series corresponds to a different exchanged operator, the energies $E_{n}$ determine the anomalous dimensions, and the coefficients in the series determine the OPE coefficients. We also determine the small and large $\mathcal{J}$ behavior of the defect correlators and the OPE data.

### 5.1 Extracting OPE data

In a 1d CFT, the conformal block expansion of a four-point function in the $12\to 34$ channel is given by [69]

$$ \displaystyle\braket{O_{1}(t_{1})O_{2}(t_{2})O_{3}(t_{3})O_{4}(t_{4})} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{t_{21}^{\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}}t_{43}^{\Delta_{3}+\Delta_{4}}}\left(\frac{t_{42}}{t_{41}}\right)^{\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}}\left(\frac{t_{41}}{t_{31}}\right)^{\Delta_{3}-\Delta_{4}} \displaystyle\times\sum_{\Delta}p_{\Delta}\chi^{\Delta}{{}_{2}F_{1}}(\Delta+\Delta_{2}-\Delta_{1},\Delta+\Delta_{3}-\Delta_{4},2\Delta,\chi). $$

Here, we take the order of the operators to be $t_{1}<t_{2}<t_{3}<t_{4}$ , in which case $0<\chi<1$ . We will restrict our attention to four-point correlators in which $O_{1}^{\dagger}=O_{3}$ and $O_{2}^{\dagger}=O_{4}$ or $O_{1}^{\dagger}=O_{4}$ and $O_{2}^{\dagger}=O_{3}$ , in which case we may choose a basis of primaries $O_{k}$ such that they satisfy the orthogonality condition $\braket{O_{k}O_{k^{\prime}}^{\dagger}}\propto\delta_{kk^{\prime}}$ , and the OPEs in the $12\to 34$ channel take the form $O_{1}O_{2}\sim\sum_{k}\frac{\mathcal{C}_{O_{1}O_{2}O_{k}}}{\mathcal{N}_{O_{k}O_{k}^{\dagger}}}O_{k}$ , $O_{3}O_{4}\sim\sum_{k}\frac{\mathcal{C}_{O_{3}O_{4}O_{k}}}{\mathcal{N}_{O_{k}O_{k}^{\dagger}}}O_{k}^{\dagger}$ . The sum over $\Delta$ in (5.1) is then a sum over the primaries $O_{k}$ with $\Delta=\Delta_{k}$ and $p_{\Delta}=\mathcal{C}_{O_{1}O_{2}O_{k}}\mathcal{C}_{O_{3}O_{4}O_{k}^{\dagger}}/\mathcal{N}_{O_{k}O_{k}^{\dagger}}$ .

We will study the conformal block expansions of the defect correlators in (2.13)-(2.14) in the “light-heavy” $\to$ “light-heavy” channels, in which case the exchanged operators appearing in the OPEs of both “light-heavy” pairs of the external operators have large charge and large conformal dimension. When multiple of the external and exchanged operators have large conformal dimensions, the conformal blocks simplify. In particular, two asymptotic expansions of the hypergeometric function that will be useful are

$$ \displaystyle{{}_{2}F_{1}}(\alpha,\beta,L+\gamma,\chi) \displaystyle=1+\frac{\alpha\beta}{L}\chi+O\left(\frac{1}{L^{2}}\right), \displaystyle{{}_{2}F_{1}}(L+\alpha,\beta,L+\gamma,\chi) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(1-\chi)^{\beta}}\left(1+\frac{\beta(\alpha-\gamma)}{L}\frac{\chi}{1-\chi}+O\left(\frac{1}{L^{2}}\right)\right). $$

The first expansion follows from the series definition ${{}_{2}F_{1}}(a,b,c,\chi)\equiv 1+\frac{ab}{c}z+\frac{a(a+1)b(b+1)}{c(c+1)}z^{2}+\ldots$ , and is relevant when $\Delta=\Delta_{1}+O(1)=\Delta_{4}+O(1)$ are large in (5.1). Eq. (5.7) is in the form of a conformal block expansion. Let us denote the primaries appearing in the OPE of $Z^{J}$ and $Z$ by $[Z^{J}Z]_{n}$ , the operators appearing in the OPE of $\bar{Z}$ and $\bar{Z}^{J}$ by $[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}$ , and their dimension by $\Delta_{n}$ . Here $n=0,1,2\ldots$ is (for the moment) simply a label to distinguish the different operators, ordered by increasing conformal dimension. For instance, the lowest primaries are $[Z^{J}Z]_{0}\equiv Z^{J+1}$ and $[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{0}\equiv\bar{Z}^{J+1}$ . We take the primaries to satisfy $[Z^{J}Z]_{n}^{\dagger}=[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}$ and $\braket{[ZZ^{J}]_{n}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n^{\prime}}}\propto\delta_{nn^{\prime}}$ .

We can now read off the OPE data of $[Z^{J}Z]_{n}$ and $[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}$ by matching (5.7) to the general form of the conformal block expansion of $\braket{Z^{J}Z\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}}$ given in (5.1). Identifying $\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{4}=J$ , $\Delta_{2}=\Delta_{3}=1$ and $\Delta=\Delta_{n}$ , and simplifying the conformal blocks using (5.2) with the identification $\alpha=\beta=\Delta_{n}+1-J$ , $\gamma=2(\Delta_{n}-J)$ and $L=2J$ , we arrive at

$$ \displaystyle\braket{Z^{J}(t_{1})Z(t_{2})\bar{Z}(t_{3})\bar{Z}^{J}(t_{4})} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{t_{21}^{J+1}t_{43}^{J+1}}\left(\frac{t_{42}t_{31}}{t_{41}^{2}}\right)^{J-1}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathcal{C}_{Z^{J}Z[Z^{J}Z]_{n}}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}}}{\mathcal{N}_{[Z^{J}Z]_{n}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}}}\chi^{\Delta_{n}} \displaystyle\hskip 113.81102pt\times\left(1+\frac{(\Delta_{n}+1-J)^{2}}{2J}\chi+O(1/g^{2})\right). $$

We can now compare (5.8) with (5.7) term-by-term, and read off the OPE data. To normalize the OPE coefficients by the norms of each of the operators, we note $\mathcal{N}_{Z\bar{Z}}=\frac{4g}{\pi}\left(1-\frac{3}{8\pi g}+\ldots\right)$ , which follows from (2.17)-(2.18). Then, for the lowest operator, we find

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{0} \displaystyle=J+1, \displaystyle\frac{|\mathcal{C}_{Z^{J}ZZ^{J+1}}|^{2}}{\mathcal{N}_{Z\bar{Z}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J+1}\bar{Z}^{J+1}}} \displaystyle=g\pi c^{2}+\frac{\pi}{2}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}+\frac{3c^{2}}{8}+O(1/g). $$

This reproduces the OPE data that we used to fix the constants of integration of $G_{Z\bar{Z}}$ and $G_{\bar{Z}Z}$ in Section 4.2.2. Meanwhile, the higher terms in the conformal block expansion produce the new OPE data:

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{n} \displaystyle=J+1+E_{n}, \displaystyle\frac{|\mathcal{C}_{Z^{J}Z[Z^{J}Z]_{n}}|^{2}}{\mathcal{N}_{Z\bar{Z}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}\mathcal{N}_{[ZZ^{J}]_{n}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}}} \displaystyle=2f(E_{n})\frac{E_{n}+1}{E_{n}}, $$

where $n=1,2,3,\ldots$ . In (5.9) and (5.10), we used $\mathcal{C}_{\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}}=\mathcal{c}^{*}_{Z^{J}Z[Z^{J}Z]_{n}}$ , which follows from reflection positivity of the dCFT. Because the simplified form of the conformal block in (5.2) is valid when $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\ll L$ , the OPE data in (5.10) is reliable as long as $\Delta_{n}-J\ll J\sim\sqrt{\lambda}$ . In the strict large charge limit, where the charge $J$ and string tension $\frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{2\pi}$ are taken to infinity, (5.10) gives the OPE data of an infinite tower of non-protected operators.

As a non-trivial check, we can also extract OPE data from $\braket{Z(t_{1})Z^{J}(t_{2})\bar{Z}(t_{3})\bar{Z}^{J}(t_{4})}$ , in which we switch the relative order of $Z$ and $Z^{J}$ . $$ \displaystyle\braket{Z(t_{1})Z^{J}(t_{2})\bar{Z}(t_{3})\bar{Z}^{J}(t_{4})} \displaystyle=\frac{4g\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}/\pi}{t_{21}^{J+1}t_{43}^{J+1}}\left(\frac{t_{42}}{t_{31}}\right)^{1-J}\chi^{J+1}G_{Z\bar{Z}}(\chi^{-1}), \displaystyle=\frac{4g\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}/\pi}{t_{21}^{J+1}t_{43}^{J+1}}\biggr[\left(g\pi c^{2}\left(1-\frac{2}{J}\frac{\chi}{1-\chi}\right)+\frac{\pi}{2}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}\right)\frac{\chi^{J+1}}{(1-\chi)^{2}} \displaystyle+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}\frac{2f(E_{n})(E_{n}+1)}{E_{n}}\frac{\chi^{J+1+E_{n}}}{(1-\chi)^{E_{n}+2}}+O(1/g)\biggr]. $$

We want to match (5.12) to the general form of the conformal block expansion in (5.1). We again denote the primaries appearing in the OPE of $Z$ and $Z^{J}$ by $[ZZ^{J}]_{n}\equiv[Z^{J}Z]_{n}$ and in the OPE of $\bar{Z}$ and $\bar{Z}^{J}$ by $[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}$ . $$ \displaystyle\braket{Z(t_{1})Z^{J}(t_{2})\bar{Z}(t_{3})\bar{Z}^{J}(t_{4})}=\frac{1}{t_{21}^{J+1}t_{43}^{J+1}}\left(\frac{t_{42}}{t_{31}}\right)^{1-J}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathcal{C}_{ZZ^{J}[ZZ^{J}]_{n}}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}}}{\mathcal{N}_{[ZZ^{J}]_{n}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}}}\frac{\chi^{\Delta_{n}}}{(1-\chi)^{\Delta_{n}+1-J}} \displaystyle\ \hskip 170.71652pt\times\left(1-\frac{(\Delta_{n}+1-J)^{2}}{2J}\frac{\chi}{1-\chi}+O(1/g^{2})\right). $$

We can now compare (5.13) with (5.12) term-by-term. For the lowest operator, we find

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{0} \displaystyle=J+1, \displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{C}_{ZZ^{J}Z^{J+1}}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}\bar{Z}^{J+1}}}{\mathcal{N}_{Z\bar{Z}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J+1}\bar{Z}^{J+1}}} \displaystyle=g\pi c^{2}+\frac{\pi}{2}\frac{1-c^{2}}{\mathbb{E}(c^{2})}+\frac{3c^{2}}{8}+O(1/g). $$

For the higher terms in the conformal block expansion, we find

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{n} \displaystyle=J+1+E_{n}, \displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{C}_{ZZ^{J}[ZZ^{J}]_{n}}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}}}{\mathcal{N}_{Z\bar{Z}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}\mathcal{N}_{[ZZ^{J}]_{n}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}}} \displaystyle=(-1)^{n+1}\frac{2f(E_{n})(E_{n}+1)}{E_{n}}, $$

for $n=1,2,3,\ldots$ . Eqs. (5.14)-(5.15) match (5.9)-(5.10) as long as $\mathcal{C}_{ZZ^{J}[Z^{J}Z]_{0}}=\mathcal{C}_{Z^{J}Z[ZZ^{J}]_{0}}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{ZZ^{J}[Z^{J}Z]_{n}}=(-1)^{n+1}\mathcal{C}_{Z^{J}Z[ZZ^{J}]_{n}}$ , for $n=1,2,\ldots$ . This is a consequence of parity, assuming $[Z^{J}Z]_{n}$ is odd for $n=2,4,\ldots$ and even otherwise. These parities of the exchanged operators are consistent with the observation that in the generalized free field limit (i.e., $g\to\infty$ , which can be probed via the $J/g\to 0$ limit of the large charge results) composite primaries can be constructed out of $J+1$ copies of $Z$ and $0,2,3,4,\ldots$ derivatives (thus, the operators $[ZZ^{J}]_{n}$ for $n>0$ contain $n+1$ derivatives), but no primary can be constructed using a single derivative because $Z^{J}\partial Z\sim\partial Z^{J+1}$ is a descendent. See Appendix D.2 for more details.

The OPE data derived in this section come with a caveat. When extracting OPE data from the conformal block expansion of a four-point function, if one does not make sure to disentangle the contributions of operators with the same quantum numbers, the extracted OPE data will in general be averages over the degenerate operators.3333 33 Indeed, part of the motivation to focus on the $\braket{ZZ^{J}\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}}$ correlator instead of the other scalar correlators is to reduce this issue of “operator mixing.” As discussed in [19] in the analysis of the $J=1$ four-point functions, at leading order in $1/g$ the operators on the Wilson line behave like generalized free fields, and there is a unique composite primary transforming in the rank $2$ symmetric traceless representation that can be constructed out of two copies of the elementary scalar field and a given even number of derivatives. Moreover, this composite operator does not mix with any other operators. However, as we discuss in Appendix D.2, for $J>1$ there are multiple composite primaries transforming in the rank $J+1$ symmetric traceless representation that can be constructed out of $J+1$ copies of the elementary scalar field and a given number of derivatives, if the number of derivatives is sufficiently large. Therefore, on general grounds we would expect the OPE data in (5.10) and (5.15) to be “mixing-averaged.” On the other hand, since we can precisely match the series representations of the four-point functions to the conformal block expansion, it is possible that the operator mixing is not relevant in the large charge limit. It would be good to understand this issue better.

### 5.2 Defect correlators and OPE data at small and large $\mathcal{J}$

In this section we examine the small $\mathcal{J}$ and large $\mathcal{J}$ behavior of the defect correlators derived in Section 4 and of the OPE data derived in Section 5.1.

#### Small $\mathcal{J}$ .

We first consider the defect correlators in the regime $1\ll J\ll g$ , in which case $\mathcal{J}$ is small. The series in (2.30)-(2.31) and (4.54)-(4.57) allow us to determine with minimal effort the small $c^{2}$ expansions of the defect correlators, which can be converted to small $\mathcal{J}$ expansions using the Taylor series relating $\mathcal{J}$ and $c^{2}$ in this regime:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J} \displaystyle=\pi c^{2}+\frac{3\pi c^{4}}{8}+\frac{15\pi c^{6}}{64}+O(c^{8}), \displaystyle c^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\pi}\mathcal{J}-\frac{3}{8\pi^{2}}\mathcal{J}^{2}+\frac{3}{64\pi^{3}}\mathcal{J}^{3}+O\left(\mathcal{J}^{4}\right). $$

We begin by determining the behavior of $E_{n}$ when $c^{2}$ is small. Qualitatively, the $E_{n}$ will be spaced approximately uniformly with unit separation, and deviations will be small in $c^{2}$ as long as $|n|$ is not too large. We can make this precise by determining the expansion of $E_{n}$ as a series in $c^{2}$ . Recall that $E_{0}=1$ exactly for all $c$ . Meanwhile, the divergence of $\rho(E)$ in (2.28) at $E=1$ makes determining the series expansion of $E_{n}$ for $n\neq 0$ directly from (2.27) a bit subtle, because naively expanding $\rho(E)$ in small $c^{2}$ and then integrating from $1$ to $E_{n}$ order by order yields divergent integrals at each order. Therefore, we rewrite (2.27) in terms of an integral that runs from $E_{n}$ to infinity, instead of from $1$ to $E_{n}$ , in order to avoid the problematic point $E=1$ :3434 34 To arrive at (5.18), we used the following pair of results $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{dE}{\sqrt{E^{2}-1}\sqrt{E^{2}+c^{2}-1}}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbb{K}(1-c^{2}),$ $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{E^{2}-1}{\sqrt{E^{2}-1}\sqrt{E^{2}+c^{2}-1}}-1\right]dE$ $\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{E}(1-c^{2}).$ (5.17)

$$ \displaystyle E_{n}-\int_{E_{n}}^{\infty}\left[\frac{E^{2}-\mathbb{E}(c^{2})/\mathbb{K}(c^{2})}{\sqrt{E^{2}-1}\sqrt{E^{2}+c^{2}-1}}-1\right]dE \displaystyle=\frac{\pi}{2\mathbb{K}(c^{2})}(1+|n|). $$

For fixed $E_{n}>1$ , it is now safe to expand the integrand in small $c^{2}$ and then integrate order by order, which yields rational functions of $E_{n}$ at each order. Writing $E_{n}=1+|n|+E_{n}^{(1)}c^{2}+E_{n}^{(2)}c^{4}+E_{n}^{(3)}c^{6}+\ldots$ , we can then determine the $E_{n}^{(i)}$ by matching powers of $c^{2}$ on both sides of (5.18). We ultimately find

$$ \displaystyle E_{0} \displaystyle=1, \displaystyle E_{n} \displaystyle=1+|n|-\frac{|n|+1}{4}c^{2}-\frac{(|n|+1)(5n^{2}+10|n|-4)}{64|n|(|n|+2)}c^{4} \displaystyle\hskip 50.07669pt-\frac{(|n|+1)(11n^{2}+22|n|-12)}{256|n|(|n|+2)}c^{6}+\ldots.\hskip 85.35826pt(n\neq 0) $$

The above series expansion is reliable as long as $|n|\ll 1/c^{2}$ .

Given the series expansion of $E_{n}$ , it is straightforward to expand the summands in (2.30)-(2.31) and (4.54)-(4.57) in small $c^{2}$ and evaluate the sums order by order. For instance, the first two terms for the small $c^{2}$ expansion of the defect correlators are given explicitly by:

$$ \displaystyle G_{1}(\chi) \displaystyle=1+\frac{c^{2}}{4}\left[\frac{(-2+\chi+\chi^{3})\log|1-\chi|}{\chi}-\frac{(2+\chi(\chi-2))(1-\chi+\chi^{2}\log|\chi|)}{(\chi-1)^{2}}\right]+O(c^{4}), \displaystyle G_{2}(\chi) \displaystyle=\frac{g\pi c^{2}\chi^{2}}{(1-\chi)^{2}}+\frac{c^{2}}{4(\chi-1)^{3}}\biggr[(1-\chi)(1+\chi^{2})(\chi+(1-\chi)^{2})\log|1-\chi| \displaystyle\hskip 42.67912pt+\chi^{3}(4-3\chi+\chi^{2})\log|\chi|\biggr]+O(c^{4}), \displaystyle G_{3}(\chi) \displaystyle=g\pi c^{2}\chi^{2}+\frac{c^{2}}{4(1-\chi)^{2}}\biggr[\chi(1-\chi)(1-2\chi+\chi^{2}) \displaystyle\hskip 42.67912pt+(1-\chi)^{3}(1+\chi+2\chi^{2})\log|1-\chi|+\chi^{3}(4-5\chi+2\chi^{2})\log|\chi|\biggr]+O(c^{4}), \displaystyle G_{4}(\chi) \displaystyle=1+c^{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{\chi}\right)\log|1-\chi|-1\right]+O(c^{4}). $$

Using the same procedure, it is relatively easy to determine the first few higher order corrections to the defect correlators. Instead of providing explicit expressions, we summarize the type of functions that appear in the expansion up to order $c^{10}$ , which may potentially be useful if one were to try to identify a suitable ansatz to “‘bootstrap” these or related correlators. At order $c^{2n}$ , the $G_{i}(\chi)$ are sums of products of the polylogarithm function $\text{Li}_{s}$ 3535 35 Recall that rational functions and the logarithm are special cases with polylogarithmic order $0$ and $1$ : $\text{Li}_{0}(z)=\frac{z}{1-z}$ and $\text{Li}_{1}(z)=-\log(1-z)$ such that the sum of the polylogarithmic orders of any of the products of polylogarithmic functions is less than or equal to $n$ . For instance, for the first few terms in the small $c^{2}$ expansion, the combinations of polylogarithms of “highest order” are logarithms at order $c^{2}$ , products of pairs of logarithms at order $c^{4}$ , and terms schematically of the form $\text{Li}_{3}$ , $\log\cdot\text{Li}_{2}$ and $\log^{3}$ appearing at order $c^{6}$ . However, not every product of polylogarithms “allowed” by the above rule appears at a given order. For instance, there is no $\text{Li}_{2}$ term at $c^{4}$ , and no $\text{Li}_{4}$ or $\text{Li}_{2}^{2}$ terms at $c^{8}$ .

We can also determine the small $\mathcal{J}$ expansion of the OPE data of the operators exchanged in the light-heavy channel of $\braket{ZZ^{J}\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}}$ , which were determined for finite $\mathcal{J}$ in (5.14)-(5.15). The first few terms in the expansions of the conformal dimensions are:

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{0} \displaystyle=J+1, \displaystyle\Delta_{n} \displaystyle=J+\left(2+n-\frac{n+1}{4\pi}\mathcal{J}+O(\mathcal{J}^{2})\right)+O(1/g), $$

The first few terms in the expansions of the OPE coefficients are:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{C}_{ZZ^{J}Z^{J+1}}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}\bar{Z}^{J+1}}}{\mathcal{N}_{Z\bar{Z}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J+1}\bar{Z}^{J+1}}} \displaystyle=g\left(\mathcal{J}-\frac{3}{8\pi}\mathcal{J}^{2}+O(\mathcal{J}^{3})\right)+\left(1-\frac{3\mathcal{J}}{8\pi}+O(\mathcal{J}^{2})\right)+O(1/g^{2}) \displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{C}_{ZZ^{J}[ZZ^{J}]_{n}}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}}}{\mathcal{N}_{Z\bar{Z}}\mathcal{N}_{Z^{J}\bar{Z}^{J}}\mathcal{N}_{[ZZ^{J}]_{n}[\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{J}]_{n}}} \displaystyle=(-1)^{n+1}\left(n+2-\frac{(n+2)(2n-1)}{4\pi n}\mathcal{J}+O(\mathcal{J}^{2})\right)+O(1/g). $$

In (5.25) and (5.27), $n=1,2,3,\ldots$ . Note that $\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{0}+2$ when $\mathcal{J}=0$ , which again corresponds to the fact that there is no composite primary in the generalized free field limit constructed out of $J+1$ copies of $Z$ and a single derivative (i.e., the $n=1$ operator corresponds in the free limit to a primary built out of $Z$ and $Z^{J}$ and two derivatives).

Finally, we note that an alternative approach to probing the defect correlators in the $1\ll J\ll g$ regime is to first take $J$ finite and expand in $1/g$ (which is the usual strong coupling expansion of the Wilson line dCFT that can be studied using Witten diagrams on the AdS2 dual string), and only then take $J$ to be large. We show in Appendix D that the results of the finite charge analysis match the large charge results in (5.21)-(5.27).

#### Large $\mathcal{J}$ .

The other limiting case of the defect correlators that is natural to consider is the regime $1\ll g\ll J$ , in which case $\mathcal{J}$ is large. The series in (2.30)-(2.31) and (4.54)-(4.57) allow us to determine the leading behaviors of the defect correlators as $\mathcal{J}\to\infty$ or, equivalently, $c^{2}\to 1$ . We note for convenience the asymptotic expansions relating $\mathcal{J}$ and $c^{2}$ in this regime:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J} \displaystyle=-2\log(1-c^{2})+4(2\log{2}-1)+O((1-c^{2})\log(1-c^{2})), \displaystyle c^{2} \displaystyle=1-\frac{16}{e^{2}}e^{-\frac{\mathcal{J}}{2}}+O(\mathcal{J}e^{-\mathcal{J}}). $$

We first determine the behavior of the energies, $E_{n}$ , when $\mathcal{J}\to\infty$ . Because $\mathbb{K}(c^{2})\to\infty$ as $c\to 1$ , it follows from (2.28) that, in this limit, the $E_{n}$ condense into a continuum with a smooth distribution. The density of the $E_{n}$ , normalized by the large charge, is asymptotically

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\rho(E)}{\mathcal{J}} \displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{E}{\sqrt{E^{2}-1}}+\frac{2}{\pi}\frac{\sqrt{E^{2}-1}}{E}\frac{1}{\mathcal{J}}+O(e^{-\frac{\mathcal{J}}{2}}), \displaystyle\text{as }\mathcal{J}\to\infty. $$

The fine-grained behavior of the $E_{n}$ when $\mathcal{J}\to\infty$ can also be determined from the above density. Neglecting the exponentially suppressed term in $\rho(E)$ , which is valid as long as $|n|\ll e^{\mathcal{J}}$ , we can evaluate the integral in (2.27) and the quantization condition becomes

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{J}+4}{2\pi}\sqrt{E_{n}^{2}-1}-\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan\left(\sqrt{E_{n}^{2}-1}\right)+O(e^{-\mathcal{J}/2}) \displaystyle=|n|. $$

This lets us determine $E_{n}$ in various regimes. When $|n|\ll\mathcal{J}$ (i.e., $E\approx 1$ ), the $E_{n}$ may be expanded in $1/\mathcal{J}$ :

$$ \displaystyle E_{n} \displaystyle=1+\frac{2\pi^{2}n^{2}}{\mathcal{J}^{2}}-\frac{2\pi^{4}n^{4}}{\mathcal{J}^{4}}-\frac{64\pi^{4}n^{4}}{3\mathcal{J}^{5}}+\frac{4\pi^{6}n^{6}}{\mathcal{J}^{6}}+O(1/\mathcal{J}^{7}). $$

When $\mathcal{J}\ll|n|\ll e^{\mathcal{J}}$ (i.e., $E_{n}\gg 1$ ), the $E_{n}$ may be expanded in $1/|n|$ :

$$ \displaystyle E_{n} \displaystyle=\frac{2\pi|n|}{4+\mathcal{J}}+\frac{2\pi}{4+\mathcal{J}}+\frac{\mathcal{J}-4}{4\pi|n|}+\frac{4-\mathcal{J}}{4\pi n^{2}}+O(1/|n|^{3}). $$

Finally, when $|n|\sim\mathcal{J}$ (i.e., $E_{n}\sim 1$ ), we may write $n=\eta\mathcal{J}$ and expand in $1/\mathcal{J}$ :

$$ \displaystyle E_{n} \displaystyle=\sqrt{1+4\pi^{2}\eta^{2}}+\frac{8\pi\eta(-2\pi\eta+\arctan(2\pi\eta))}{\sqrt{1+4\pi^{2}\eta^{2}}}\frac{1}{\mathcal{J}} \displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt+\frac{8(2\pi\eta-\arctan(2\pi\eta))(2\pi\eta-\arctan(2\pi\eta)+16\pi^{3}\eta^{3})}{(1+4\pi^{2}\eta^{2})^{\frac{3}{2}}}\frac{1}{\mathcal{J}^{2}}+O(1/\mathcal{J}^{3}). $$

The leading term in (5.34) precisely matches the expression for the energy of fluctuations about the $c^{2}=1$ string in the BMN limit, which was derived in [8]. In particular, [8] found that the fluctuations have energies $\omega_{p}=\sqrt{1+p^{2}}$ and argued that the boundary conditions fix the momenta to be $p_{n}=\frac{n\sqrt{\lambda}}{2J}$ with $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ . We note that in (5.34), $2\pi\eta=\frac{2\pi ng}{J}=\frac{n\sqrt{\lambda}}{2J}.$
